3 · Harness Engineering 2 / 8 · Charter, plan & board

PROJECT.md, PLAN.md, TASK.md & MEMORY.md

A harness is never finished, only proven so far. These files keep that honest: PROJECT.md states what the harness promises, PLAN.md maps each incident to a control and a proof, TASK.md shows which proofs have passed and which gaps are still open. The first three are conventions, wired in through CLAUDE.md. MEMORY.md is Claude's own.

PROJECT.md convention — the harness charter

Unlike the other two workflows, the question here is not “what does the product do?” but “what must be true for every engineer and every session?”, and which mechanism makes it true.

Golden template

golden template 
# PROJECT.md — {{Project}} harness charter

## Purpose
{{What the product does, in one or two sentences.}}

## What the harness must guarantee, for every engineer and every session
- {{Guarantee}} — enforced by {{hook | permission | MCP tool | skill | plugin}}

## Not the harness's job
- {{Concern handled elsewhere}} — {{where}}

## Glossary
- "{{term}}": {{meaning in this codebase}}

Filled example — CityFix

PROJECT.md 
# PROJECT.md — CityFix harness charter

## Purpose
CityFix lets residents report potholes, broken streetlights and other city issues,
and routes them to repair crews by priority.

## What the harness must guarantee, for every engineer and every session
- No credential reaches a committed file — enforced by a PreToolUse hook
- Priority scores come from the documented formula, never hand arithmetic — enforced by the issue-priority-scorer skill
- Triage and retention rules are looked up, not remembered — enforced by the cityfix-docs-rag MCP server
- A new engineer gets all of this with one command — enforced by the cityfix-toolkit plugin

## Not the harness's job
- Code formatting taste — gofmt runs automatically, humans review the rest
- Feature design — each feature gets its own plan

## Glossary
- "priority score": base + 2 x duplicates - 0.5 x days open (capped at 10), per docs/policies/triage-policy.md
- "auto-escalate": a score of 15 or more goes to the emergency response queue

PLAN.md convention — incident, gap, control, proof

Harness work starts from something that went wrong, so the plan is shaped like an incident report rather than a feature spec. Every control carries the command that proves it works, written before you build it. The last section says plainly what the plan does not cover.

Golden template

golden template 
# PLAN.md — {{Harness change}}
Status: {{draft | approved by <name> on <date>}}

## Incident {{n}} — {{one line}}
- Gap: {{nothing enforced | nothing discoverable | nothing observable}}
- Control: {{the hook, permission, tool or skill that closes it}}
- Proof: {{command that shows it works}} → {{expected output}}

## Ship order
1. {{control}}

## Out of scope
- {{What we are not fixing here}}

## Known gaps
- {{What this plan does not cover, said plainly}}

Filled example — CityFix

PLAN.md 
# PLAN.md — Close the two recurring gaps
Status: approved by the platform lead, 2026-08-12

## Incident 1 — a session nearly committed the real Mapbox key to .env.production
- Gap: nothing enforced
- Control: PreToolUse hook that blocks Edit and Write on secret-looking paths
- Proof: echo '{"tool_input":{"file_path":".env"}}' | .claude/scripts/block-secret-file-writes.sh; echo $?
  → prints 2. A normal path such as internal/priority/score.go prints 0.

## Incident 2 — three engineers hand-computed the priority score; two got the age decay wrong
- Gap: nothing discoverable
- Control: issue-priority-scorer skill, shipped in the cityfix-toolkit plugin
- Proof: from a clean checkout, install the plugin and ask for the score of a pothole with 6 duplicates open 4 days
  → the skill runs the script and prints "Final score: 15.0" and "AUTO-ESCALATE".

## Ship order
1. Hook and script  2. Skill  3. Docs RAG server  4. Plugin bundle

## Out of scope
- Secret scanning in CI. That belongs to the pipeline team.

## Known gaps
- The hook matches Edit|Write only. A Bash command such as `echo KEY=x > .env` is not covered.
- cityfix-docs-rag returns the first 400 characters of each policy file.

TASK.md convention — the board of controls

One line per control, each with its proof. A line is ticked only when the proof printed what the plan said it would. Anything unproven or known-leaky stays open and visible, which is how a harness avoids claiming more safety than it has.

Golden template

golden template 
# TASK.md — {{Harness change}}
Plan: PLAN.md. Edited by the main session only.

- [ ] 1. {{Control to build}} — verify: `{{command}}` → {{expected output}}

## Open
- [ ] {{Known gap}} — verify when fixed: `{{command}}` → {{expected output}}

Filled example — CityFix, after the first build

TASK.md 
# TASK.md — Close the two recurring gaps
Plan: PLAN.md. Edited by the main session only.

- [x] 1. block-secret-file-writes.sh — verify: pipe '{"tool_input":{"file_path":".env"}}' into it → exit code 2
- [x] 2. Register the PreToolUse hook — verify: /hooks lists it under PreToolUse for Edit|Write
- [x] 3. issue-priority-scorer skill — verify: `go run scripts/priority_score.go --issue-type pothole --duplicates 6 --days-open 4` → Final score 15.0, AUTO-ESCALATE
- [x] 4. cityfix-docs-rag server — verify: /mcp shows it connected; get_stats → "2 policy document(s) indexed."
- [x] 5. cityfix-toolkit plugin — verify: clean checkout, /plugin install, then /agents lists both agents

## Open
- [ ] Cover Bash writes to secret files — verify when fixed: pipe '{"tool_input":{"command":"echo KEY=x > .env"}}' into the new hook → exit code 2
- [ ] Raise the RAG snippet limit above 400 characters before triage-policy.md outgrows one paragraph

MEMORY.md auto-written by Claude — what Claude learned building it

Written by Claude, not by you, into ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/. Illustrative: the real notes are in Claude's own words, and they stay on your machine.

~/.claude/projects/cityfix/memory/MEMORY.md (illustrative — written by Claude) 
# Memory index — cityfix
- [Hook input is JSON on stdin](hook-stdin.md) — read tool_input with jq; don't rely on environment variables
- [Age decay is capped](age-decay-cap.md) — min(days x 0.5, 10); two engineers forgot the cap
- [RAG snippet limit](rag-snippet-limit.md) — cityfix-docs-rag returns only the first 400 chars per policy file

Where each file lives in the plugin story. PROJECT.md, PLAN.md and TASK.md belong to this repo: they describe this product and this piece of work. The plugin ships the reusable parts (agents, the skill, hooks, the MCP server) so other repos get them. MEMORY.md never leaves your machine.

3 · Harness Engineering 3 / 8 · Hooks

.claude/settings.json — golden template & example official

JSON, not markdown — hooks are shell commands fired at fixed lifecycle events, guaranteed to run whether or not the model "remembers" to.

Golden template

golden template 
{
  "model": "{{model}}",
  "permissions": {
    "allow": ["{{auto-approved tools/commands}}"],
    "ask": ["{{tools requiring approval}}"]
  },
  "hooks": {
    "{{PreToolUse|PostToolUse|Stop|...}}": [
      {
        "matcher": "{{tool name or regex}}",
        "hooks": [
          { "type": "command", "command": "{{script — exit 0 to allow, 2 to block}}" }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

Filled example

.claude/settings.json 
{
  "model": "claude-sonnet-5-5",
  "permissions": {
    "allow": ["Read", "Grep", "Glob", "Bash(go test ./...)"],
    "ask": ["Edit", "Write", "Bash(*)"]
  },
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Edit|Write",
        "hooks": [
          { "type": "command", "command": ".claude/scripts/block-secret-file-writes.sh" }
        ]
      }
    ],
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Write|Edit",
        "hooks": [
          { "type": "command", "command": "jq -r '.tool_input.file_path // empty' | grep -E '\\.go$' | xargs -r gofmt -w" }
        ]
      }
    ],
    "Stop": [
      {
        "hooks": [
          { "type": "command", "command": "echo '[session end] tick TASK.md only for controls whose proof passed' >&2" }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
.claude/scripts/block-secret-file-writes.sh 
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
file_path="$(jq -r '.tool_input.file_path // empty')"
if [[ -z "$file_path" ]]; then
  exit 0
fi
case "$file_path" in
  *.env|*.env.*|*secrets*|*credentials*|*mapbox*key*)
    echo "Blocked: '$file_path' looks like a secrets file. Edit it by hand if this is intentional." 1>&2
    exit 2
    ;;
  *) exit 0 ;;
esac

Both hooks read the tool call the same way: as JSON on standard input, parsed with jq. What this does not catch: the matcher is Edit|Write, so a Bash command like echo KEY=x > .env sails past it. That gap is written down as an open line in TASK.md rather than hidden. Tighten it with a second hook matching Bash, or with permission deny rules.

Filled example — the working server behind it

tools/cityfix-docs-rag/package.json 
{
  "name": "cityfix-docs-rag-server",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "type": "module",
  "main": "index.js",
  "scripts": { "start": "node index.js" },
  "dependencies": { "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk": "^1.5.0" }
}
tools/cityfix-docs-rag/index.js 
#!/usr/bin/env node
// Keyword/TF-IDF search over local policy docs — no embedding API key required.
import { Server } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/index.js";
import { StdioServerTransport } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/stdio.js";
import { CallToolRequestSchema, ListToolsRequestSchema } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/types.js";
import fs from "node:fs";
import path from "node:path";

const DOCS_DIR = process.env.DOCS_DIR || path.join(process.cwd(), "docs/policies");

function tokenize(text) { return text.toLowerCase().match(/[a-z0-9]+/g) || []; }

function loadCorpus() {
  const files = fs.readdirSync(DOCS_DIR).filter((f) => f.endsWith(".md"));
  return files.map((file) => {
    const raw = fs.readFileSync(path.join(DOCS_DIR, file), "utf8");
    return { file, raw, tokens: tokenize(raw) };
  });
}

function scoreDoc(queryTokens, doc) {
  const freq = {};
  for (const t of doc.tokens) freq[t] = (freq[t] || 0) + 1;
  let score = 0;
  for (const q of queryTokens) score += freq[q] || 0;
  return score / Math.sqrt(doc.tokens.length || 1);
}

function ragSearch(query, topK = 3) {
  const corpus = loadCorpus();
  const qTokens = tokenize(query);
  return corpus
    .map((doc) => ({ file: doc.file, score: scoreDoc(qTokens, doc), snippet: doc.raw.slice(0, 400) }))
    .sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score).slice(0, topK).filter((r) => r.score > 0);
}

const server = new Server({ name: "cityfix-docs-rag", version: "1.0.0" }, { capabilities: { tools: {} } });

server.setRequestHandler(ListToolsRequestSchema, async () => ({
  tools: [
    { name: "rag_query", description: "Answers a question using CityFix's triage and data-retention policies.",
      inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { question: { type: "string" } }, required: ["question"] } },
    { name: "get_stats", description: "Returns how many policy documents are indexed.",
      inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: {} } },
  ],
}));

server.setRequestHandler(CallToolRequestSchema, async (request) => {
  const { name, arguments: args } = request.params;
  if (name === "rag_query") {
    const results = ragSearch(args.question, 3);
    if (results.length === 0) return { content: [{ type: "text", text: `No policy matched "${args.question}".` }] };
    const text = results.map((r) => `### ${r.file}\n${r.snippet}...`).join("\n\n");
    return { content: [{ type: "text", text }] };
  }
  if (name === "get_stats") {
    return { content: [{ type: "text", text: `${loadCorpus().length} policy document(s) indexed.` }] };
  }
  throw new Error(`Unknown tool: ${name}`);
});

await server.connect(new StdioServerTransport());
docs/policies/triage-policy.md (part of the corpus) 
# Issue triage policy

Priority score = (base score by issue type) + (2 × number of duplicate reports)
− (0.5 × days since first reported, capped at 10).

Base scores: pothole = 5, broken streetlight = 4, water main leak = 9, graffiti = 2,
downed tree = 8.

Any issue scoring 15 or higher is auto-escalated to the emergency response queue.
docs/policies/data-retention.md (the rest of the corpus) 
# Citizen data retention policy

Reporter contact info is retained for 90 days after an issue is marked resolved,
then purged. Photos attached to reports are retained for 2 years for infrastructure
planning, with reporter identity stripped after 90 days.

Two documents is a deliberately small corpus for this guide — the point of a real cityfix-docs-rag deployment is that this folder grows without the MCP server's code changing at all. Compare this server to Agentic Engineering's policy-rag: same pattern, same ~60 lines, completely different corpus — that repetition is the point, not an accident. Once you've built one, you've effectively learned to build all of them.

What's actually inside ./agents/

The manifest above only points at paths — here's what a teammate installing this plugin actually receives, in full. Both agents built specifically for CityFix, independent of Agentic Engineering's PawMatch agents:

.claude-plugin/agents/cityfix-issue-reviewer.md 
---
name: cityfix-issue-reviewer
description: Use proactively after any change to files under internal/priority/ or internal/reports/. Reviews for hardcoded priority weights that should trace back to policy, citizen PII retained past policy, and missing escalation logic. Read-only — never edit.
tools:
  - Read
  - Grep
  - Glob
model: sonnet
---

You are a policy-compliance reviewer for a citizen issue-reporting platform.
For every change, check specifically for:
1. Any hardcoded priority weight or score — re-query the cityfix-docs-rag MCP server to confirm it still matches docs/policies/triage-policy.md, and flag drift if it doesn't
2. Reporter PII retained past the documented 90-day window
3. Missing auto-escalation logic for issues scoring 15 or higher
Report findings as a short bullet list with file:line references. Do not fix — only report.
.claude-plugin/agents/cityfix-test-writer.md 
---
name: cityfix-test-writer
description: Use after the feature author adds or changes priority-scoring logic. Writes the boundary-case unit tests required by testing-rules.md. Read-write, but only inside internal/priority/priority_test.go.
tools:
  - Read
  - Write
  - Bash(go test ./...)
model: sonnet
---

You write Go table-driven tests only, for priority-scoring logic. For any new or
changed scoring rule, add a test at the escalation boundary (score 14 vs 15), one
clearly-low-priority case, and one clearly-high-priority case. Run go test ./...
yourself before reporting done.

What's actually inside ./skills/

The skill this whole case study's second incident is about — bundled here so a new engineer gets it without ever being told it exists:

.claude-plugin/skills/issue-priority-scorer/SKILL.md 
---
name: issue-priority-scorer
description: Use when asked to compute or explain an issue's priority score for triage.
---

# Issue Priority Scoring Playbook

Given issue type, duplicate report count, and days since first reported, run
`scripts/priority_score.go` rather than estimating the arithmetic by hand:

    go run scripts/priority_score.go --issue-type pothole --duplicates 6 --days-open 4

1. Any score of 15 or higher must trigger auto-escalation — never suppress this.
2. Always show the script's output, not just the final number.

See `reference/base-scores.md` for the documented base score per issue type.
.claude-plugin/skills/issue-priority-scorer/scripts/priority_score.go 
// Computes an issue's priority score per docs/policies/triage-policy.md.
// Referenced by SKILL.md so Claude runs it directly instead of estimating
// the arithmetic itself.
package main

import (
	"flag"
	"fmt"
	"math"
)

var baseScores = map[string]float64{
	"pothole":             5,
	"broken_streetlight":  4,
	"water_main_leak":     9,
	"graffiti":            2,
	"downed_tree":         8,
}

func main() {
	issueType := flag.String("issue-type", "", "issue type key, e.g. pothole")
	duplicates := flag.Int("duplicates", 0, "number of duplicate reports")
	daysOpen := flag.Float64("days-open", 0, "days since first reported")
	flag.Parse()

	base, ok := baseScores[*issueType]
	if !ok {
		fmt.Printf("Unknown issue type: %s\n", *issueType)
		return
	}

	decay := math.Min(*daysOpen*0.5, 10)
	score := base + float64(*duplicates)*2 - decay

	fmt.Printf("Base score:      %.1f\n", base)
	fmt.Printf("Duplicate bonus: +%.1f\n", float64(*duplicates)*2)
	fmt.Printf("Age decay:       -%.1f\n", decay)
	fmt.Printf("Final score:     %.1f\n", score)
	if score >= 15 {
		fmt.Println("AUTO-ESCALATE: score meets emergency response threshold")
	}
}

This is the point of a plugin as a Harness Engineering artifact: a teammate never has to author any of these files themselves, or even be told they exist — /plugin install is the entire onboarding step.

.claude-plugin/marketplace.json 
{
  "name": "civic-platform-marketplace",
  "owner": "civic-platform-team",
  "plugins": [
    {
      "name": "cityfix-toolkit",
      "source": "./",
      "description": "Issue review, testing, priority scoring, and policy RAG search for CityFix"
    }
  ]
}

The exact manifest field names here are still evolving on Anthropic's side — treat this as the right shape, and check code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins for the current schema before shipping it to a team.

3 · Harness Engineering 6 / 8 · Prompts

How you actually ask for this

Harness Engineering prompts talk about the environment itself — guardrails, reusability, distribution — not a single feature. Compare the verbs: “add a hook so this can never happen again,” not “fix this one instance.” And each prompt ends on proof: how will we know the control works?

Set-up (once)

Prompt · bootstrap the project memory

Run /init to scan this repo, then rewrite the generated CLAUDE.md so it documents: CityFix, a Go 1.22 service using Postgres with PostGIS for issue geolocation, deployed on AWS ECS. Start with a Project context section containing only the line @PROJECT.md. Add a Do-not section forbidding committing a real Mapbox/GIS API key inline — it must come from the environment — and changing the issue-priority formula without running its tests first. Add a Tooling line noting the team's Claude Code setup ships as the cityfix-toolkit plugin, and a Working files section: PLAN.md maps incidents to controls, TASK.md is ticked only by the main session after a proof command passes.

→ produces: CLAUDE.md
Prompt · personal, local-only overrides

Create a CLAUDE.local.md and add it to .gitignore. Note that my local Postgres+PostGIS runs on port 5433 via Docker, my local Mapbox key is a personal sandbox key and never the production one, and I run go test ./internal/priority/... for fast iteration on scoring logic only.

→ produces: CLAUDE.local.md, updated .gitignore
Prompt · the harness charter

Create PROJECT.md for CityFix as a harness charter: a two-line purpose; a list of what the harness must guarantee for every engineer and every session, each with the mechanism that enforces it (secret writes blocked by a PreToolUse hook, priority scores from the issue-priority-scorer skill, policy lookups through the cityfix-docs-rag MCP server, one-command setup through the cityfix-toolkit plugin); what is not the harness's job; and a glossary defining priority score and auto-escalate.

→ produces: PROJECT.md

Plan and board

Prompt · incidents to controls

Switch to Plan mode. Here are two incidents: a session nearly committed the real Mapbox key into .env.production, and three engineers hand-computed the priority score and two got the age decay wrong. For each, write the gap (nothing enforced, nothing discoverable), the control that closes it, and a proof command with its expected output. Add a ship order, what is out of scope, and a Known gaps section that says plainly what this plan does not cover. Do not build anything yet. When I approve, save it as PLAN.md.

→ produces: PLAN.md (after you approve)
Prompt · the board

From PLAN.md create TASK.md: one line per control with its proof command and expected output, an Open section for every known gap, and a header saying only the main session edits it. Tick a line only after you have run its proof and seen the expected output.

→ produces: TASK.md

Build the controls

Prompt · guardrails

Add a PreToolUse hook in .claude/settings.json that runs .claude/scripts/block-secret-file-writes.sh before every Edit or Write. Write that script to read the tool-call JSON from stdin with jq and exit 2 for any path matching *.env, *secrets*, *credentials*, or anything that looks like a Mapbox API key file. Add a PostToolUse hook that runs gofmt on any edited .go file, reading the path from the same stdin JSON, and a Stop hook that reminds me to tick TASK.md only for controls whose proof passed. Set the model and require approval for Edit/Write/Bash, but auto-allow Read/Grep/Glob and go test ./.... Then run the proof from PLAN.md and show me the output.

→ produces: .claude/settings.json, block-secret-file-writes.sh, and the proof output
Prompt · a reusable tool for every future agent

I need a RAG server for our triage and data-retention policies, exposed over MCP, so any current or future agent can query it — not just this session. Build tools/cityfix-docs-rag as a Node.js MCP server using @modelcontextprotocol/sdk, scoring the corpus with term-frequency matching so we never need an embedding API key. Register it in .mcp.json alongside our GitHub server. Prove it: /mcp should show it connected and get_stats should report 2 policy documents.

→ produces: tools/cityfix-docs-rag/*, .mcp.json
Prompt · package it so it outlives this repo

Bundle the issue reviewer, the test-writer, the priority-scoring skill, our hooks, and the cityfix-docs-rag MCP server into one installable plugin called cityfix-toolkit, so every future project — not just this one — can adopt the whole harness with a single /plugin install instead of five manual steps. Leave PROJECT.md, PLAN.md and TASK.md out of it: they belong to this repo.

→ produces: plugin.json, marketplace.json

Prove it and keep it honest

Prompt · prove the environment, not the feature

Run /memory, /agents, and /mcp so I can confirm the harness itself is loaded and connected — not any particular task's output. Then print the full repo tree so I can sanity-check nothing's missing before a new teammate installs this.

→ produces: a check of the harness, independent of any feature built on top of it
Prompt · close a known gap

Take the first Open line in TASK.md: Bash writes to secret files bypass our Edit|Write hook. Add a second PreToolUse hook matching Bash that rejects commands redirecting into secret-looking paths, using the same stdin-JSON approach. Write its proof first, show it failing, then make it pass, and only then tick the line.

→ produces: a second hook and script, and a ticked TASK.md line
Prompt · review what Claude remembered

Run /memory and open this project's auto-memory folder. List what you saved while we built the harness. Tell me which notes only matter on my machine and which the whole team needs. Propose the shared ones as additions to PLAN.md or CLAUDE.md, but do not edit anything until I approve.

→ produces: a review only. Nothing is written until you approve
3 · Harness Engineering 7 / 8 · Case study

The two mistakes that kept happening — until the harness made them structurally unlikely

Distinct on purpose from the other two case studies: this isn't a feature request from a product backlog, it's two recurring incidents that had nothing to do with any single task. Simple to state. The fix for both is environment design, not a one-off patch — which is the whole point of Harness Engineering as its own workflow type.

The problem

  • Incident 1: an engineer's Claude Code session was one accepted diff away from committing the city's real Mapbox API key into .env.production. Nobody had told that particular session not to — nothing was watching.
  • Incident 2: in the same week, three different engineers each independently re-derived the issue-priority-scoring formula by hand instead of finding the existing script, and two of the three got the age-decay term wrong — one issue that should have auto-escalated didn't.

Neither is a feature to build. Both are harness gaps: incident 1 is nothing enforced; incident 2 is nothing discoverable. A code review comment or a Slack reminder fixes the mistake once, for one person. A harness fixes the class of mistake, for everyone, permanently.

The fix

  • For incident 1 — enforcement: the block-secret-file-writes.sh PreToolUse hook (the settings.json page) makes the mistake structurally impossible rather than just documented against — it blocks the write before it happens, for any engineer, in any session, whether or not they've read this guide.
  • For incident 2 — discoverability: bundling issue-priority-scorer into the cityfix-toolkit plugin (the plugin page) means a new or existing engineer gets the skill automatically the moment they install the toolkit — not by remembering it exists or asking around.

How the planning files carried it

  1. PLAN.md records each incident as gap → control → proof, with a ship order and a Known gaps section.
  2. TASK.md turns every control into one line with its proof command. A line is ticked only when the command prints what the plan expected.
  3. Five lines get ticked. Two stay open on purpose: Bash writes bypass the Edit|Write hook, and the RAG server's 400-character snippet will eventually truncate a longer policy.
  4. While building, Claude saved a lesson to its own MEMORY.md: hooks receive the tool call as JSON on stdin. That note stays on your machine; the fix itself (both hooks parse stdin with jq) is what travels with the plugin.

Proving both fixes actually work

  1. Test the guardrail in isolation — solves incident 1: chmod +x .claude/scripts/block-secret-file-writes.sh, then echo '{"tool_input":{"file_path":".env"}}' | .claude/scripts/block-secret-file-writes.sh; echo $? → must print 2. A normal file must print 0.
  2. Test discoverability as a brand-new engineer would experience it — solves incident 2: from a clean checkout, claude, then /plugin marketplace add ./.claude-plugin and /plugin install cityfix-toolkit@civic-platform-marketplace. Now ask, in plain language, "what's the priority score for a pothole with 6 duplicate reports open 4 days?" — it should surface and use the skill without you pointing Claude Code at anything.
  3. Confirm the rest of the bundle rode along too: /memory, /agents, /mcp — the reviewer, the test-writer, and the cityfix-docs-rag server should all show as connected, even though neither incident was about them.

If all three checks pass: the specific mistake from incident 1 is now structurally unlikely for any engineer, and the wasted time from incident 2 is gone, because the fix travels with the plugin instead of living in one person's memory. That's the distinct shape of a Harness Engineering win — not a shipped feature, but a class of mistake that stops recurring. Notice too that this entire example — stack, incidents, agents, skill, RAG corpus — shares nothing with ClauseCheck in Agentic Coding or PawMatch in Agentic Engineering. Same three underlying patterns, three unrelated problems.

What passing does not mean. These three checks prove the two incidents cannot recur the same way. They do not prove secrets are safe in general: an agent could still write a key with a shell redirect. That is why TASK.md keeps an Open line for it instead of a tick. A harness is only as trustworthy as its list of known gaps.

3 · Harness Engineering 8 / 8 · Diagrams

CityFix — Architecture, Functional & Workflow

Same three views, one more workflow type: now the diagrams have to show an environment wrapping an app, not a pipeline processing a task. Same static-PNG caveat applies — motion is suggested, not literal.

1 · Architecture

  1. At the center: the core Go service — just application code, internal/priority and internal/reports.
  2. Wrapping it: the always-on layer. settings.json's PreToolUse hook guards every write attempt, unconditionally — it doesn't wait to be asked.
  3. Also in that layer: the cityfix-docs-rag MCP server, which reads docs/policies/*.md and answers rag_query() calls about triage and retention policy.
  4. Also in that layer: the cityfix-issue-reviewer subagent (read-only, reviews diffs) and the issue-priority-scorer skill (callable on demand).
  5. Wrapping all of that: the plugin — cityfix-toolkit — the only thing a new engineer actually has to install to get every inner layer at once.
  6. Notice the direction of dependency: the core service doesn't know the harness exists. The harness wraps around it, not the other way around — that's what "environment design" means, drawn concretely.
  7. Compare this to Agentic Engineering's architecture diagram: there, the agent team sat beside the app. Here, the harness is drawn around it — same underlying primitives (agents, tools), a completely different relationship to the code being protected.

2 · Functional

  1. Flow 1 (enforcement): an agent attempts an Edit or Write.
  2. The PreToolUse hook fires automatically — this isn't optional or something the agent chooses to invoke.
  3. The hook checks the file path against a pattern: does it look like *.env or contain "key"?
  4. If yes: exit code 2 — blocked, and Claude Code is told why. If no: exit code 0 — the write proceeds normally.
  5. Flow 2 (discoverability): a new engineer clones the repo and runs /plugin install cityfix-toolkit.
  6. In one step, they now have the skill, both agents, the hooks, and the MCP server — all present, none individually installed.
  7. They ask a plain-language question ("what's the priority score for...") and the skill fires on its own, because its description field matched their intent — they never had to know the skill's name existed.
  8. These two flows share no code and fire on completely different triggers — a write attempt vs. a plain question. That's the point: "harness" isn't one mechanism, it's a category of mechanisms serving the same goal.

3 · Workflow (incident to structural fix)

  1. Incident: something goes wrong twice, independent of any single task — here, a near-miss secret leak and inconsistent priority scoring.
  2. Plan it (PLAN.md): for each incident the engineer writes the gap (nothing enforced, nothing discoverable), the control that closes it, and the proof command with its expected output — before building anything. The plan also lists known gaps.
  3. Build once: settings.json and the hook script, the skill files, plugin.json — written a single time.
  4. Prove in isolation: run each proof from the plan — pipe fake JSON into the hook and read the exit code; install the plugin on a clean checkout, ask a question and confirm the skill fires.
  5. Tick the board (TASK.md): a line is ticked only when its proof printed the expected output. Anything that can't yet be proven, such as Bash writes bypassing the hook, stays open and visible.
  6. Prevented for every engineer: the fixed gaps now apply to anyone who ever opens this repo, not just the person who hit the original incident.
  7. Compare stage 6 here to Agentic Coding's workflow diagram, which ends at “merge.” This one ends at “this class of mistake is structurally unlikely, and the board says what still isn’t covered” — a different, and longer-lived, definition of done.
Core Reference 1 / 10 · Mental model

The layered context system

Claude Code isn't "a chatbot with file access." It's an agentic loop — read → plan → act → check — wrapped around a layered context system. Each layer loads at a different time, for a different reason. This is the conceptual foundation every file in the three workflow-type sections builds on — read this group once, deeply, and the workflow-type pages become quick reference rather than new material.

LayerFile(s)LoadedPurpose
Project memoryCLAUDE.mdEvery session, upfrontStanding facts: architecture, conventions, "never do X"
Personal overridesCLAUDE.local.mdEvery session (gitignored)Your machine-specific stuff
Path-scoped rules.claude/rules/*.mdWhen you touch matching filesNarrow conventions
Config & permissions.claude/settings.jsonEvery sessionModel choice, tool permissions, hooks
Reusable expertise.claude/skills/*/SKILL.mdOn demand, task-matchedPlaybooks, checklists, domain procedures
Delegated specialists.claude/agents/*.mdOn demand, own contextIsolated sub-tasks
External tools/data.mcp.jsonAt session start, calls on demandDBs, trackers, your RAG index
Shareable bundles.claude-plugin/plugin.jsonOn installPackages skills+agents+hooks+MCP
Session continuityNOTES.md (your convention)Manually, by you or ClaudeSurvives compaction / new sessions
Working filesPROJECT.md, PLAN.md, TASK.md (your conventions)Only when CLAUDE.md imports or mentions themStable what/why, the approved approach, the status board
Auto memoryMEMORY.md + topic files (Claude writes them)Session start, first ~200 lines of the indexLessons Claude learned from your corrections; machine-local

The single biggest mistake people make: stuffing everything into CLAUDE.md. It's always loaded, so every line is a permanent tax on every session's context. The skill is knowing what deserves to be always-loaded vs. loaded just-in-time.

Core Reference 2 / 10 · Project memory

CLAUDE.md

What it is: a markdown file at your project root. Claude Code walks up the directory tree from your working directory to the repo root, reading every CLAUDE.md it finds along the way, and concatenates them — additive, not overriding.

Where

  • ./CLAUDE.md — project root, checked into git, shared with the team
  • ./CLAUDE.local.md — same directory, gitignored, personal
  • ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md — your global preferences across all projects
  • Nested CLAUDE.md in subdirectories — applies when work touches that subtree (monorepos)

Generate a starting point: run /init inside Claude Code — it scans the repo and drafts one you then edit.

What to put in it

  • Architecture in 3–5 lines ("API Gateway → 6 microservices via gRPC, Postgres per service, Kafka for events")
  • Tech stack and why ("Spring Boot 3, not Micronaut — team expertise")
  • Commands Claude should use (make test, not npm test if that's wrong)
  • Hard rules ("never touch /infra/terraform without asking")
  • Review checklist expectations (idempotency keys, structured logging fields)

What NOT to put in it: full API docs (link instead), one-off task instructions, anything you wouldn't repeat to a new hire twice.

CLAUDE.md 
# CLAUDE.md — Payments Ledger Service

## Architecture
Java 21 / Spring Boot 3 microservice. Exposes REST + gRPC. Postgres (ledger DB),
Kafka topic `ledger.events.v1` for downstream settlement. Deployed on EKS.

## Conventions
- All monetary values: `long` cents, never `double`/`float`.
- Every write endpoint requires an `Idempotency-Key` header — see `IdempotencyFilter`.
- Tests: JUnit5 + Testcontainers. Run with `./gradlew test`. No mocking the DB layer.
- Commits: Conventional Commits. PR must reference a Jira ticket (LEDGER-XXXX).

## Do not
- Do not modify `schema.sql` directly — use Flyway migrations in `db/migration/`.
- Do not call external payment providers directly from this service; use `payment-gateway-client`.

This is the compact version — see the Agentic Coding CLAUDE.md page for the fuller one with a Project context import.

Core Reference 3 / 10 · Delegation

.claude/agents/*.md — Subagents

A subagent is a markdown file with YAML frontmatter, run in its own context window, with its own system prompt, restricted toolset, and independent permissions. This is how you stop one giant session from doing exploration, coding, and review all in one polluted context.

Where: .claude/agents/ (project, shared via git) or ~/.claude/agents/ (personal). Create interactively with /agents.

Built-in, for free: Explore (read-only, fast, runs on Haiku), Plan (gathers context before proposing a strategy), general-purpose (explore + modify). Claude routes to these automatically.

Frontmatter that matters: name, description (write it behaviorally — add "use proactively" to trigger it automatically), tools (narrow allow-list), disallowedTools, model, permissionMode, maxTurns.

.claude/agents/payments-security-reviewer.md 
---
name: payments-security-reviewer
description: Use proactively after any change to files under src/payments/. Reviews for PCI-relevant issues, idempotency gaps, and missing audit logging. Read-only — never edit.
tools:
  - Read
  - Grep
  - Glob
model: sonnet
---

You are a security-focused reviewer for a payments microservice.
For every change, check specifically for:
1. Missing idempotency keys on state-changing endpoints
2. Card/account data logged in plaintext
3. Missing audit trail entries for balance-changing operations
Report findings as a short bullet list with file:line references. Do not fix — only report.

A read-only reviewer like this cannot accidentally edit what it's reviewing — that's the point of the narrow tools list, not an accident. See the Agentic Engineering agents page for a second, read-write example (the test-writer) and how the two work together in a pipeline.

Core Reference 4 / 10 · Just-in-time expertise

.claude/skills/*/SKILL.md

Skills are the newest, most important primitive. A Skill is a folder with a SKILL.md (frontmatter + instructions) plus optional scripts, templates, or reference files. Claude scans the name + description of every skill every session (cheap), but only pulls the full body into context when the task actually matches — progressive disclosure. A project can have 50 skills without bloating every session; a 5,000-line CLAUDE.md would.

Where: .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md (project) or ~/.claude/skills/ (personal). Invoke with /skill-name or let Claude auto-trigger it.

Skills follow an open standard (Agent Skills spec) — the same SKILL.md works in Claude.ai, the API, and other adopting tools.

.claude/skills/kafka-capacity-check/SKILL.md 
---
name: kafka-capacity-check
description: Use when asked to size Kafka partitions/brokers for a target throughput, or to review an existing topic's capacity assumptions.
---

# Kafka Capacity Sizing Playbook

Given a target events/sec and average message size:
1. Compute required partition count: throughput ÷ per-partition-throughput-budget (~10MB/s/partition unless told otherwise).
2. Recommend replication factor 3 for anything touching money movement; RF 2 for pure telemetry.
3. Flag if consumer group lag would exceed 2x partition count (rebalancing risk).
4. Always show the formula, not just the number.

See `reference/broker-sizing-table.md` for AWS MSK instance-type throughput numbers.

Skill vs. Subagent vs. Hook

PrimitiveWhat it is
SkillOn-demand knowledge/procedure the main agent loads into its own context.
SubagentOn-demand delegation to a separate context window — isolation, not just knowledge.
HookDeterministic enforcement outside the model entirely — fires every time, no matter what Claude "decides."

Core Reference 5 / 10 · Deterministic control

Hooks — not a markdown file

Hooks are shell commands (or HTTP calls) that fire at fixed lifecycle events, configured as JSON in .claude/settings.json. They exist because you can't rely on a model to remember to run a formatter or block a dangerous command every single time — a hook guarantees it.

Common events: SessionStart, PreToolUse (before any tool runs — can block/rewrite), PostToolUse (after completion — auto-format, log, feedback), UserPromptSubmit, Stop, SubagentStop.

.claude/settings.json 
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Edit|Write",
        "hooks": [
          { "type": "command", "command": "scripts/block-env-file-writes.sh" }
        ]
      }
    ],
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Write|Edit",
        "hooks": [
          { "type": "command", "command": "jq -r '.tool_input.file_path // empty' | xargs -r npx prettier --write" }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

Exit code 2 from a PreToolUse hook blocks the tool call and feeds the reason back to Claude. This is the layer you'd point to if an interviewer asks "how would you stop Claude Code from ever committing a .env file" — the answer is a hook, not a prompt instruction.

How a hook sees the tool call: Claude Code passes it as JSON on standard input, so a hook script parses tool_input (for example .tool_input.file_path) with jq. Don't depend on environment variables for this.

Core Reference 6 / 10 · The outside world

.mcp.json — MCP & your RAG answer

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the open protocol that lets Claude Code call tools outside its built-in set — a database, an issue tracker, a browser, or your own RAG pipeline. Servers are configured in .mcp.json at the project root (commit it) or added via claude mcp add.

.mcp.json 
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "github": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-github"],
      "env": { "GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN": "${GITHUB_TOKEN}" }
    },
    "ledger-rag": {
      "command": "node",
      "args": ["./tools/rag-mcp-server/dist/index.js"]
    }
  }
}

Which RAG pattern to reach for

  • Lightweight / static corpus → a Skill with reference files Claude greps on demand. No vector DB needed.
  • Real RAG / large, changing corpus → a small MCP server wrapping your embedding + vector store, exposing tools like rag_query, rag_search, index_document.

The tool description field in a custom MCP server is the only signal the model uses to pick the right tool — write it precisely. For a standalone agent/RAG service outside the CLI: that's the Claude Agent SDK — same primitives, embedded programmatically in your own service.

Core Reference 7 / 10 · Distribution

.claude-plugin/plugin.json — Plugins

A plugin bundles skills, agents, hooks, and MCP servers into something installable via a marketplace:

plugin structure 
my-plugin/
├── .claude-plugin/
│   ├── plugin.json        # required manifest
│   └── marketplace.json   # if publishing to a marketplace
├── commands/               # slash commands
├── agents/                 # subagent definitions
├── skills/                 # skill folders (each with SKILL.md)
├── hooks/                  # hook configs
├── .mcp.json               # bundled MCP servers
└── README.md

Install with /plugin install <name>@<marketplace>. Knowing the shape — and that it's plugin.json, not "PLUGIN.md" — is worth having straight if it comes up.

Core Reference 8 / 10 · Session continuity

NOTES.md — the "journal.md" pattern

There's no Anthropic-mandated journal.md. What's real is a widely-used "Document & Clear" discipline: before context gets long or you compact/clear a session, dump the current plan and decisions to a plain markdown file — PROGRESS.md, NOTES.md, whatever you call it. A long session is not a reliable record of what was decided; a file is.

NOTES.md 
# NOTES.md — Assessment session, Deriv

## Decisions
- Chose MCP server over embedding RAG directly into a Skill: corpus is large + changes daily.
- Idempotency key strategy: UUID v4 client-generated, stored with 24h TTL in Redis.

## Open questions
- Confirm whether settlement events need exactly-once or at-least-once semantics.

Narrating "I'm going to write our decisions to a NOTES.md as we go" is exactly the kind of engineering-leadership habit a Head of Engineering interview is trying to surface — and it's current Claude Code best practice too. See the Agentic Engineering NOTES.md page for how this becomes a decision journal that sits beside PLAN.md and TASK.md, and the next page for which of these files are official.

Core Reference 9 / 10 · What is official

MEMORY.md, PLAN.md, TASK.md, PROJECT.md

Four names that look like siblings but aren't. Exactly one of them is a Claude Code feature. The other three are conventions that work well, if you wire them in.

FileStatusWritten byClaude reads it when…What goes in it
MEMORY.mdauto-written by ClaudeClaudeA session starts (first ~200 lines of the index)Lessons from your corrections, one line each, linking to topic files
PROJECT.mdconventionYouCLAUDE.md contains @PROJECT.md, then every sessionPurpose, scope, why we said no to things, glossary
PLAN.mdconventionYou, drafted with Claude in Plan modeA prompt, CLAUDE.md or an agent body says “read PLAN.md first”The approved approach for one piece of work: objective, steps, owners, gates
TASK.mdconventionThe main sessionSame: only when pointed atA checklist with a verify command per step. The status board
NOTES.mdconventionYou or ClaudeSame: only when pointed atDecisions with reasons, open questions, verification evidence

Where each one lives

where things live 
my-repo/
├── CLAUDE.md          imports @PROJECT.md, mentions PLAN.md / TASK.md / NOTES.md
├── PROJECT.md         stable: what and why              (checked in)
├── PLAN.md            per feature: the approved plan    (checked in, replaced per feature)
├── TASK.md            per feature: status board         (checked in, deleted when merged)
└── NOTES.md           per feature: decisions + evidence (checked in)

~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/
├── MEMORY.md          index Claude maintains            (NOT in git, this machine only)
└── <topic>.md         one file per lesson

How a convention file actually gets read

Claude Code has no “look for PLAN.md” behaviour. A file is read if it is imported (@PROJECT.md inside CLAUDE.md loads it at session start) or named (a line like “read PLAN.md before starting” in CLAUDE.md, a prompt or a subagent's body makes Claude open it when it matters).

CLAUDE.md — wiring convention files in 
## Project context
@PROJECT.md                 # always loaded: stable what and why

## Working files
- Read PLAN.md before starting any task. It is the approved approach.
- TASK.md is the status board. Only the main session edits it.
- Record why-decisions in NOTES.md.

Which file does this fact belong in?

If the fact is…It goes in
True on every task, every machine, for every contributor, and shortCLAUDE.md
The reason the product exists, its scope, or why we refused somethingPROJECT.md
How we will build this one feature, and who does which stepPLAN.md
Whether step 3 is done and how to check itTASK.md
Why we chose X over Y, or what a reviewer foundNOTES.md
Something Claude learned from being corrected on your machineMEMORY.md (Claude's job). If the whole team needs it, copy it into CLAUDE.md
Only true on your laptop (port, personal key)CLAUDE.local.md

Plan mode is not PLAN.md. Plan mode is a built-in permission mode: Claude reads and proposes, but can't edit until you approve. PLAN.md is a file you may choose to save that plan into, so other sessions and subagents can read it. One is a mode, the other is a document.

How sure is this page? That CLAUDE.md, rules, agents, skills, hooks, .mcp.json and plugins are Claude Code features, and that @path imports work, is well established. Auto memory (MEMORY.md, the 200-line load, the /memory toggle) is newer, and this guide describes it from summaries of Anthropic's docs. Run /memory in your own install and read Anthropic's current Claude Code memory documentation before relying on the details. PROJECT.md, PLAN.md, TASK.md and NOTES.md are community conventions, not Anthropic specifications.

Guide · Your actual setup

Doing all of this from VS Code

Everything above is just files in your project folder. They work identically no matter which surface you use — none of it changes by workflow type, either. What changes is only how you invoke Claude Code and review its work.

Two ways Claude Code shows up in VS Code

  1. The official Claude Code extension — Ctrl+Shift+X / Cmd+Shift+X → search "Claude Code" → the one published by Anthropic. Bundles its own CLI, gives inline diffs, plan review, @-mentions with line ranges, conversation history. Anthropic's recommended surface.
  2. The standalone CLI — npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code, run claude in VS Code's integrated terminal. Same engine; needed if an environment expects the raw command or scriptable/headless behavior.

Install both before the assessment. Set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY as a shell env var in advance — either surface accepts it, and launching VS Code with code . from that terminal inherits it automatically.

Where the conventions live in the panel

  • Press / for the slash-command surface: /memory, /agents, /mcp, /hooks, /plugin.
  • Or just create CLAUDE.md, .claude/agents/reviewer.md, .mcp.json directly in the file explorer — often faster once you know the shape.
  • The Spark icon (✦) — editor toolbar, Activity Bar, or status bar — opens the panel.

One deliberate choice for a recording: leave approval-gated permission mode on (claudeCode.initialPermissionMode) and narrate your review of each diff before accepting. Auto-accept removes the exact moment you get to demonstrate judgment.

Guide · Deriv, Head of Engineering

The assessment-day playbook

A recorded, think-aloud assessment isn't testing whether you can write a for-loop. It's testing whether you can direct an AI tool the way you'd direct a senior engineer, and narrate architectural reasoning in real time.

Before you join

  1. Install Claude Code and confirm it runs — don't debug installation on camera.
  2. Set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY as a shell env var in advance; confirm subscription login is active if you use that instead.
  3. Keep a minimal CLAUDE.md template ready to fill in fast.
  4. Do one full test round-trip beforehand — scaffold something, edit a file.
  5. Have a scratch repo with git init already done; commit as you go.
  6. Decide your narration rhythm: state intent before every prompt, state what you're verifying after.

During the assessment

  1. Restate the requirement, sketch the architecture before touching Claude Code.
  2. Write the CLAUDE.md first, narrating why — the single highest-leverage first five minutes.
  3. Use Plan mode and say why you want to see the approach before it touches files.
  4. Save the approved plan to PLAN.md and, if the work is bigger than one sitting, a TASK.md checklist. Say aloud that these are conventions, not Claude Code features, and add a line to CLAUDE.md pointing at them.
  5. Delegate isolation/repetition to a subagent, and say so — tie tool choice to a security/process rationale.
  6. Verify, don't just accept — run tests, read diffs, push back out loud when warranted.
  7. Narrate production considerations unprompted — observability, idempotency, rollback, DORA metrics.
  8. Keep a running NOTES.md of decisions and open questions as you go.

An assessment requiring "your API key ready" very likely includes a task where you write or wire up something live. Given how small most live tasks are, you'll most likely be operating in Agentic Coding or a light Agentic Engineering pass (the first two workflow types) rather than building a whole harness live — but naming which one you're in, out loud, is itself a strong signal of maturity, and it's exactly the vocabulary this guide gives you.
